questions.q: Why does this lesson describe governance as 'a tax paid on every change to prevent the expensive ones'?
options: Because Salesforce literally charges a monetary fee for every governed deployment

Because governance review steps catch a small number of genuinely expensive mistakes, but every change -- including the overwhelming majority that were never going to be that mistake -- pays the same review cost unless the process is designed to tell them apart
Because governance only applies to financial-services Salesforce orgs
Because governance review boards are staffed exclusively by external auditors
questions.explain: The review cost is paid uniformly across changes regardless of their actual risk, unless the process specifically tiers changes by risk -- which is exactly the design gap this lesson focuses on.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect governance vs. agility to Lesson 12's centralized-vs-decentralized design tension?
options: They are unrelated topics covered only because they appear in the same chapter
Governance always requires full decentralization to function properly

Governance vs. agility is described as the process-level version of the same tension: heavy governance centralizes risk-catching in a review process, and the agility cost is the same bottleneck that over-centralization produces
Agility is only relevant to decentralized orgs, never to centralized ones
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames this as the process-level version of Lesson 12's tension -- the same bottleneck failure mode (teams waiting on a queue for low-risk changes) shows up again here in the form of a change advisory board.

questions.q: What does this lesson say 'shadow IT' actually signals, beyond being a compliance problem?
options: Nothing -- shadow IT is purely a discipline failure that should always be addressed by punishing the responsible team
That the organization's security review has expired
That the org needs to purchase more Salesforce licenses
Data about where the governance process doesn't match the actual risk of the changes it's gating -- a prompt to re-tier the process, not only a violation to crack down on
questions.explain: The lesson frames shadow IT as a predictable response to governance that stopped matching actual risk, and recommends reading it as a design signal rather than treating it solely as a compliance violation to punish.

questions.q: What lever does this lesson recommend pulling before adding more manual review steps to a governance process?
options: Investing in CI/CD automation with real automated test coverage, which can catch more actual defects faster without adding to anyone's wait time
Hiring more reviewers to staff additional review board meetings
Removing all review steps entirely regardless of change risk
Requiring every change to go through two separate change advisory boards instead of one
questions.explain: The lesson specifically argues that a well-built automated pipeline can catch more defects than an added layer of human sign-off, without increasing wait time -- the better lever than simply adding more manual review.

questions.q: What does 'risk tiering,' as described in this lesson, actually do to a governance process?
options: It applies the exact same review process uniformly to every change regardless of its risk level
It sorts changes by actual risk level, so a low-risk change moves through a lightweight or automated path while a high-risk change still gets the full review gate
It eliminates governance entirely for changes made by senior admins
It requires every change to be reviewed by the full change advisory board twice
questions.explain: Risk tiering is the lesson's proposed fix for the mismatch that produces shadow IT -- matching governance intensity to actual risk instead of treating every change identically.
